topic: Chinese civilisation grew up along the Yellow and Yangtze rivers; the Shang (from about 1600 BC) left the first Chinese writing.
In 221 BC the Qin unified China into an empire; for two thousand years dynasties rose and fell, with long periods of division between them.
Under the Han, Tang and Song, China led the world in technology (paper, printing, gunpowder, the compass) and in trade along the Silk Road.
After the last dynasty fell in 1911 came a republic, civil war and Japanese invasion; the Communists founded the People's Republic in 1949.

Prehistory: Homo erectus lived in China over a million years ago; 'Peking Man' is one of the best-known finds.
Farming began around 7000 BC: millet in the north, rice in the Yangtze valley.
Later Chinese history remembered this time through legends of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, and of Yu the Great taming the floods.
Ancient China: Tradition names the Xia as the first dynasty; the Shang (about 1600–1046 BC) left oracle bones bearing the earliest Chinese writing.
The Zhou overthrew the Shang and justified it by the 'Mandate of Heaven', the idea that heaven withdraws support from unjust rulers.
As Zhou power faded, the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods saw rival states, and the thinkers of the 'Hundred Schools', including Confucius and Sun Tzu.
Early imperial China: The state of Qin, reformed by Shang Yang along Legalist lines, conquered its rivals; in 221 BC Ying Zheng became Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor.
The Qin standardised writing, weights and coins, and began the Great Wall, but fell soon after his death.
The Han dynasty (202 BC–AD 220) lasted four centuries, made Confucianism the state ideology and opened the Silk Road after Zhang Qian's missions.
Han China produced Sima Qian's history, Cai Lun's paper and Zhang Heng's seismoscope; Wang Mang briefly usurped the throne (AD 9–23).
Six Dynasties: The Yellow Turban Rebellion (184) broke the Han; China split into the Three Kingdoms of Wei, Shu and Wu.
The Jin briefly reunited China, but northern peoples overran the north (the Sixteen Kingdoms), and the country divided into Northern and Southern dynasties.
In these centuries of division Buddhism spread widely through China.
Mid-imperial China: The Sui reunited China in 589 and built the Grand Canal linking north and south.
The Tang (618–907), ruling from Chang'an, was a cosmopolitan golden age of poetry (Du Fu, Li Bai); Wu Zetian was China's only reigning empress.
The An Lushan rebellion (755–763) crippled the Tang; after its fall came the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms.
Late imperial China: The Song (960–1279) had a commercial economy, paper money, movable type and a bureaucracy chosen by examination, while the Liao, Western Xia and Jin held the north.
The Mongols under Genghis Khan and Kublai Khan conquered all of China, ruling as the Yuan dynasty.
The Ming (1368–1644) drove out the Mongols; Zheng He's treasure fleets sailed to Africa, and the Great Wall took its present form.
The Manchu Qing dynasty (1644–1912) expanded China to its largest extent but was weakened in the 19th century by the Opium Wars and the Taiping Rebellion.
Modern period: The 1911 Revolution ended the empire; Sun Yat-sen's republic soon fell to warlords, until Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists reunified much of China.
Japan seized Manchuria (1931) and invaded China in 1937; the war cost millions of lives.
Mao Zedong's Communists won the civil war and proclaimed the People's Republic in 1949; the Nationalists retreated to Taiwan.
The Great Leap Forward caused a catastrophic famine and the Cultural Revolution further chaos; from 1978 Deng Xiaoping's reforms began China's rise as an economic power.
